title: Covenant Eyes
tagline: Designing for behavior change, for people who aren't ready to ask for help yet.
headline: How do you help someone who isn't ready to ask for help?
summary: At Covenant Eyes I led the design of two features that guide people early in recovery: Commit and Reflect, and a Lessons widget.
outcomes: Commit and Reflect drove a 26% increase in adoption
The Lessons widget boosted retention by 32%
lessons: Before a feature launches, ask how you'll learn it's working besides the data
Every launch is an opportunity to receive feedback
article:
Covenant Eyes helps Christians in the US who struggle with pornography addiction. It blocks, filters, monitors, and reports screenshots to an accountability partner.

It comes as two apps. Victory Shield monitors the device, and Victory is where you manage your journey. The full value only shows up with two people: the person who wants accountability, and the partner who provides it.

![Victory Shield](content/covenant-eyes/shield.jpg)

![Victory](content/covenant-eyes/victory.jpg)

## The problem

Asking someone to hold you accountable is hard, and many people early on aren't ready. There's shame and a lot of emotional friction, so upgrading gets put off.

Free users landed on a home screen that offered them recent activity they couldn't access and a suggested course. Courses were the only useful thing there, and they were left to find their own way through them.

![The home screen free users saw](content/covenant-eyes/before.jpg)

Picture Jake. He hears about Covenant Eyes at his congregation. He's tired of breaking promises to himself and wants a way out, but he isn't ready to tell anyone yet.

> How might we help people early in the process and guide them to real recovery?

## Commit and Reflect

### Starting from recovery itself

A year-long research effort with users, licensed therapists, and recovery leadership had landed on three pillars: Clarity, Commitment, and Connection. I used them to shape the experience.

I looked at how Duolingo, Headway, and Livestrong use streaks, progress, achievements, and community. I sorted the ideas by effort and impact, then by how well they fit those three pillars.

### The first idea was too literal

My early explorations turned the path to recovery into an actual path, with badges along the way. The goal was for people opening the app to feel in control, hopeful, and not alone. I kept exploring from there, adding a progress bar, a pledge, and redesigned suggested readings.

![An early exploration of The Path](content/covenant-eyes/path.jpg)

![Badges and achievements](content/covenant-eyes/badges.jpg)

![A home screen built around a pledge](content/covenant-eyes/pledge.jpg)

### Two designers, one feature

Another designer was working on a Daily Pledge, to show people they aren't alone, while I was working on a daily reflection, to give them clarity. We were building two versions of the same moment, so we merged them into one flow.

![An early version of the merged flow: a pledge plus a self-reflection](content/covenant-eyes/merge.jpg)

Marketing wanted to convert people from the start. Product wanted to attract and keep new, free users. Working with marketing, research, and product, we agreed this feature could serve both the short and the long term.

### What people told us

With a research partner, I tested prototypes with people further along in recovery, since people early in the journey often weren't ready to talk about it. Pledges resonated. Power Ups fell flat because they were hard to grasp, so we kept going with pledges.

### A word can carry too much weight

When we showed the prototype at a company-wide meeting, the feedback was clear: in the Christian world "pledge" holds too much weight to use lightly. I sat down with the Director of Recovery, we brainstormed names, and "pledge" became "commit." That's how Commit and Reflect got its name.

![Commit and Reflect, as it shipped](content/covenant-eyes/final.jpg)

**+26%** increase in adoption.

## Lessons

### A big library with no way in

Even with just the courses, people arriving in Victory felt lost. The team saw a chance to guide them through the learning journey instead of dropping all that content in their lap.

![The course library](content/covenant-eyes/library.jpg)

Imprint, Noom, and Atomic Habits pointed toward bite-size learning. The Director of Recovery and I took inventory of every lesson, then sorted them into three journeys: men, women, and allies.

### Designing the widget

It had to save vertical space on the home page, be clear about which lesson it was showing, encourage people to tap in, and stay inside the existing design system.

![Iterations on the Lessons widget](content/covenant-eyes/iterations.jpg)

The widget lived inside a 30-day journey, so I planned for every state, including what happens when you finish everything recommended.

![Widget states across the 30-day journey](content/covenant-eyes/states.jpg)

### Read on, or come back tomorrow?

I let people keep reading. If they wanted more, they could go on to the next lesson. If they completed all the lessons, they reached a state showing just that.

![Letting people keep reading](content/covenant-eyes/agency-a.jpg)

![The state for completing all the lessons](content/covenant-eyes/done.jpg)

A usability test confirmed this was a familiar pattern. It also showed that the main call to action pulled some people away from the widget.

![Lessons on the home screen, as it shipped](content/covenant-eyes/after.jpg)

**+32%** increase in retention.

## Where it was heading

Commit and Reflect and Lessons were early pieces of a bigger plan for guided recovery in Victory, with a daily tracker and a clear view of your progress.

![The daily tracker](content/covenant-eyes/vision.jpg)

![The end goal](content/covenant-eyes/endgoal.jpg)

## What I learned

When we first launched Commit and Reflect, I forgot to put a feedback loop on it. A lot of people wanted to give feedback, but for the first two weeks we couldn't get any in, because I hadn't designed for it.

Now I ask this before a feature launches: besides the data, how am I going to learn that it's working as intended? Every launch is an opportunity to receive feedback.
